project_summary: A geolocation investigation that finds where a security-camera recording was made using only aircraft Doppler curves in its audio. The only known facts are the date, September 8, and that it was filmed somewhere in the continental US. The recording holds two faint propeller-plane Doppler curves 920 seconds apart and no other aircraft between them. The creator downloads a day of ADS-B flight data for the continental US, drops known jet types, and lays candidate observer points on a grid around each flight. CPA is the closest point of approach. For each point he computes the delayed CPA time, when the CPA sound reaches the observer, from the 3D slant distance. A DEM gives ground elevation and the speed of sound gives the delay. Speed, slant distance, CPA time, and fundamental frequency measured from each curve, plus a silence constraint between the events, cut the candidates to about 15,000. He then models the exact curve each candidate would hear from the radial velocity at emission time, scores it against the spectrogram with a locked two-event method on a 100 m grid, and ranks the best point per flight pair. A separate run on a one-minute clip with a known time ranks the same coordinate first, and Street View confirms the camera. The video ends by testing countermeasures. The description states that the code and tools are not released.

systems.name: ADS-B ingest and aircraft filtering
systems.description: Downloads every flight over the continental US for the target day with a Python scraping package, keeping whole flight paths with position, altitude, speed, timestamp, and type code. Drops known jet types using an ICAO type-code lookup table. Later cuts flight segments to the measured velocity range and, when the recording time is known, to that time window.

systems.name: Spectrogram measurement
systems.description: Finds the faint Doppler curves by zooming into the right frequency band at high resolution. Fits an ideal constant-velocity Doppler curve to each event and records generous ranges for velocity, CPA slant distance, CPA time in the audio, and fundamental frequency. Traces a very faint curve as a line.

systems.name: Acoustic geometry and propagation model
systems.description: Finds each observer's CPA to a flight and the 3D slant distance, using ADS-B altitude above sea level and DEM ground elevation. Converts distance to sound travel delay, which turns CPA time into delayed CPA time and gives the emission time the Doppler model needs.

systems.name: Candidate grid and constraint filters
systems.description: Lays observer points on a 200 m grid, first out to 10 km from each track and later only at the measured slant distance. Keeps points that hear two flights 920 seconds apart, within about 5 seconds, at the measured speeds and distances, and that hear no other flight between the two events.

systems.name: Doppler curve forward model
systems.description: For each candidate point and flight, computes the frequency the observer would hear over time. Each time step uses the radial velocity at the moment the sound was emitted, taken from interpolated ADS-B, in the Doppler equation with the measured fundamental frequency.

systems.name: Spectrogram scoring and ranking
systems.description: Scores each modelled curve by the spectrogram brightness it covers, or by distance to a traced line. Sweeps CPA time offset and fundamental frequency for event 1, locks event 2's offset to the flight geometry, refines survivors to a 100 m grid, and ranks the best point per flight pair.

systems.name: Map review and ground-truth confirmation
systems.description: Shows scored points and per-flight heat maps in QGIS, then checks the top coordinate in Google Maps Street View against the source footage.

systems.name: Countermeasure tests
systems.description: Tests whether high-pass filtering, masking noise, cuts, and phone-call compression remove the Doppler signal, by looking for the curve in the spectrogram afterwards.

milestones.title: Problem setup and finding the Doppler curves
milestones.summary: The target is a security-camera video in which nothing changes visually. The only facts given are the date, September 8, and that it was filmed in the continental US. A previous thunder-based method reached about 5 km precision. Two audio sections play and the signal is inaudible. In a spectrogram, with time on x and frequency on y, it only appears after zooming into the right frequency band and raising the resolution. It is a Doppler curve from an aircraft. A second, louder curve with harmonics follows later, and these two curves are the evidence for the search. The creator states the project took months and over 5,000 lines of code, with 50 GB Parquet files, 3D physics modelling, and countrywide DEMs.

milestones.title: Download ADS-B data and keep propeller aircraft
milestones.summary: The first idea is to keep only places that heard a plane and then another plane 920 seconds later. ADS-B data gives nearly every aircraft's position, speed, and altitude. A paid API exists, but the creator ran a Python scraping package for a few hours to get every flight over the continental US on September 8. The package downloads whole flight paths, so tracks reach Hawaii and other countries. Played with boosted frequencies, the louder curve sounds like a propeller plane. The ADS-B type code does not say propeller or jet, so he used a lookup table that does. The table has gaps, so he removed known jet types rather than keeping known propeller types.

milestones.title: Grid candidate points and compute delayed CPA times
milestones.summary: This step is shown on a small test area. Each ADS-B point of a flight has coordinates, altitude, and a timestamp. The creator lays a 200 m grid of observer points within 10 km of the flight path, a conservative limit for hearing a plane. Hearing a plane spans almost two minutes, so the event time is the CPA, which he calls closest point of arrival, when the plane is nearest and loudest. The time that matters is the delayed CPA time, when the CPA sound reaches the observer. The delay uses the 3D slant distance. ADS-B altitude is above sea level, so a DEM gives each grid point's ground elevation. In the worked example the CPA time is 22:46:34 and the delayed CPA time is 22:46:46. Repeating this for every flight gives each grid point a list of flight IDs and delayed CPA times.

milestones.title: Filter grid points by the 920-second offset
milestones.summary: For each grid point the creator checks whether any two delayed CPA times sit 920 seconds apart. The window allows about 5 seconds either way, because where the centre of a curve is measured varies. About 35,000 points pass in the test area, which is under 0.05% of the continental US land area. A football-field comparison makes the point that this filter alone cannot search the whole country.

milestones.title: Measure speed, slant distance, and CPA time from each Doppler curve
milestones.summary: Two comparison clips show that a larger frequency drop means a faster object. With constant linear velocity, velocity sets the size of the drop and CPA slant distance sets how quickly it happens. The creator fits an ideal Doppler curve over each event on the spectrogram. Event 1 fits on the right side but not the left, which matters later. He records generous ranges instead of single values. The right side fits at about 100 m/s, and 70 m/s clearly does not. CPA time keeps a few seconds of error, with a best match at 151.15 nudged to 151.13 after sliding the fundamental frequency up. The output is a measurement range for each event.

milestones.title: Apply speed, slant-distance, and silence filters
milestones.summary: Flight segments are cut to the event 1 velocity range, drawn green, and the event 2 range, drawn pink. Candidate points now sit only at the measured slant distance from each segment, not across the full 10 km grid. A point passes if it hears a green segment and then a pink segment 920 seconds later at the right distances. About 73,000 points pass, mostly in clusters at airports where traffic is dense. The recording has no other aircraft for almost 15 minutes between the events, so a silence filter removes any point that would have heard a flight in between. The thresholds are shown on screen and are conservative. About 70,000 points drop to 15,000. The creator notes that this uses up everything the simple spectrogram measurements can give.

milestones.title: Forward-model the Doppler curve from real flight geometry
milestones.summary: The measured curves are not ideal because planes change heading, speed, and altitude. Several geometries can produce the same variation, so the spectrogram cannot be inverted. Instead the creator models the exact curve each candidate point would hear from each flight's real ADS-B track and looks for the match. The heard frequency depends on radial velocity, the part of the plane's velocity toward or away from the observer. Head-on it equals the plane's speed, side-on it is zero and there is no shift. The Doppler equation takes the speed of sound c, the radial velocity v_r, and the measured fundamental frequency f0. In the worked example v_r is 0 at CPA, 7:12:30, giving 130 Hz, and 62.7 at 7:12:35, giving 109.9 Hz. These numbers fit f = f0 * c / (c + v_r) with c = 343 m/s for a receding source, which is inferred and not stated. Repeating this per time step gives a curve.

milestones.title: Correct the model for sound travel time
milestones.summary: Using the radial velocity at the hearing time is wrong and would make the search fail. The frequency heard at time t comes from the plane's velocity when it emitted the sound heard at t. So for each time step the model finds where the plane was when it emitted that sound, takes the radial velocity there, and applies the Doppler equation. The result is a different curve shape, not the naive curve shifted later. On the real spectrogram the emission-time curve matches and the naive curve does not. The model runs for every candidate point and every flight.

milestones.title: Score modelled curves with locked two-event scoring
milestones.summary: Each modelled curve is drawn on the spectrogram and scored by summing the brightness values it covers. Fundamental frequency and CPA time both come from measurements, so both carry error. Event 1 is placed by putting its modelled delayed CPA at the measured CPA timestamp in the audio. The scorer then sweeps a few seconds of time offset and a range of fundamental frequency and keeps the best combination. Event 2 gets its own fundamental-frequency sweep, but its time offset from event 1 is locked to what the flight geometry predicts, so a bad event 2 placement counts against the candidate. The scoring is sharp enough that on the 200 m grid the true point could sit up to 141 m away and score badly. So the survivors are resampled to 100 m, about 30,000 to 40,000 points. This is expensive, which is why the earlier filters matter.

milestones.title: Rank candidates by flight pair and inspect the top hits
milestones.summary: Each candidate has an event 1 score and an event 2 score, shown as a scatter plot where the top right is best. No single point stands out at first. Grouping by flight pair and keeping the best point per pair leaves one clear leader at 20.48, whose modelled curves cover both observed curves. The second best, about 15, is close on event 1 but badly off on event 2, and the third is worse. In QGIS the creator views the scored points, then reruns at finer resolution for only the winning flights and shows heat maps for event 1, event 2, and both combined.

milestones.title: Confirm with a one-minute known-time clip and Street View
milestones.summary: A second test uses only the first, inaudible curve, one minute of audio, with a known time of 8:37 PM UTC and the whole continental US as the search area. The same spectrogram measurement gives velocity bounds, and only flight segments at that time are kept. With one event the scores form a histogram, not a scatter plot. The curve is too faint for brightness scoring, so the creator traces it with a line and scores each modelled curve by its distance to that line. The top point matches, at the same coordinates the two-event search found, 40.87, -73.5. He generalises that a search needs either several events or a tight time, and that a city-sized area, about 0.01% of US land, allows much looser time bounds. He then zooms to the heat-map centre in QGIS, which sits at the edge of water, opens the coordinate in Google Maps, and matches a V-shaped tree line in Street View. Zooming out shows the security camera on a pole.

milestones.title: Test countermeasures
milestones.summary: A high-pass filter fails for two reasons. The Doppler curves sit in the same band as the human voice, and after high-passing, exporting to MP3, and boosting all frequencies, the curve comes back. Masking fails too, because a JBL speaker across the room had been playing a Doppler curve under the last 15 seconds of speech. Cutting the audio removes the offset between events, but one minute with a known time can still work, and phone calls give known times. In a phone-call test the JBL speaker plays a Doppler curve in another room, and the receiving phone sits under Squishmallows to block leakage. The curve survives the call's compression and noise reduction. He points out a gap in the curve around when he starts talking again, and the transcript does not make the cause clear. His suggested measures are cuts and extra noise cancellation.
